narrative.what_i_did:
The operator opened with 'Yes, continue on' after a brief inter-session handoff where the stop-hook had flagged the dispatch-branch:main refspec push and I confirmed the close hook had already resolved it (remote main and remote dispatch were both at 5a07f1e). I grounded against the prior session.json — the previous carpenter shipped the member-side family ratify modal and the useInboxRouting extraction in one cut, closing the family-mode arc end-to-end. WalletProvider was still flagged at 797 lines, one under the 800 hard limit. The natural next-up cuts named in whats_pending were field-test on a real phone, WalletProvider extraction, tree-v2 family rendering, or the operator's add-birthday-now backdated credential. The chip-form opener I surfaced offered those four; the operator picked tree-v2 family rendering — Recommended because it directly consumes the substrate we just finished and ships a visible feedback loop for the field-testing they were about to do anyway.

Before touching code I read peopleTreeLayout.ts, PeopleTree.tsx, peopleTreeLayout.test.ts, and PeopleTabBody.tsx. The existing v1 substrate was already clean: pure layout math separated from rendering, deterministic FNV-1a-hash angles so the same peer always lands in the same spot, extractPeers + extractOrgs returning typed objects with a stable angle field, a CATEGORY_COLOR vocab matching the handshake relationship leaf. The renderer used a positioned-div container with absolute-positioned SVG behind for edges (pointer-events-none) and HTML divs in front for IdentityChip nodes (so the chip primitive renders crisp instead of being re-implemented inside SVG). Adding a third ring with the same pattern was straightforward — the layout pattern was already saying 'here is how you add a new ring.'

I extended peopleTreeLayout.ts with extractFamilies plus a TreeFamily type. The function calls findFamilyUnitsForMember to find every family-unit envelope the operator is named in (a wallet can be in more than one family — birth family AND chosen family — and both surface), reads each via readFamilyUnit, computes ratification progress via familySignatureProgress threading the optional keyAliases parameter so the operator's own signature counts after key rotation, and seeds each family's angle from the family-unit envelopeId hash. The envelopeId seed matters because two families founded by the same wallet would collide on founder-pubkey hash; envelopeId is the unique cryptographic identifier so the angle stays unique per family. I added a FAMILY_UNIT_EDGE_COLOR constant that aliases CATEGORY_COLOR.family — the family-unit edge shares the family-peer-category pink so the visual reads as 'family-shaped relationship' whether you have a one-on-one handshake-with-spouse leaf or a multi-party family-unit envelope; the structural distinction is the radius and the node shape, not the color. Seven new tests cover the operator-as-founder, operator-as-non-founder-member, multi-family operator with both birth and chosen, ratification-progress counting (founder + me signed of three named), envelopeId-stable angle, and the rotated-key keyAliases bridge.

The renderer extension in PeopleTree.tsx ran in the same shape as the existing peer/org pattern. I rebalanced the three ring radii so the new family ring fits between peer and org — peers tightened from 110 to 100, family ring lands at 145, orgs pushed out from 165 to 190 — and bumped the canvas height from 420 to 460 to fit the wider footprint. Each family node is a 110-by-44 rounded rose-50 panel with a rose-300 border, the family name in semibold rose-900 on top, and an X-of-Y-signed progress line below that flips emerald-700 when the family is fully ratified and rose-700 otherwise. Family edges draw at 3px stroke width with 0.7 opacity — thicker and more present than the 2px / 0.55 peer edges so the multi-person nature of a family unit reads at a glance. Legend gains a Family-unit entry between Acquaintance and Organization with a 3-pixel-tall rose swatch.

The keyHistory plumbing was three lines of mechanical wiring: PeopleTree gained an optional myKeyHistory prop, the families useMemo builds a single-entry Map<my-genesis-pubkey, [active+previous+...]> if myKeyHistory is provided and passes it through to extractFamilies, PeopleTabBody added myKeyHistory to its Props and threaded it through to PeopleTree, and HomeScreen passes wallet.keyHistory from useWallet at the mount site. The same one-sided rotation bridge FamilyIdentitySections and FamilyRatifyModal already use — only the operator's own keyHistory is bridged because we don't have remote members' rotation chains.

Empty-state copy updated too. The 'Your mycelium tree is empty' message now says 'Make a handshake with someone, join an organization, or start a family, and they will start appearing here as branches around you' — the prior copy mentioned only handshakes and orgs, leaving the new family path uncovered. The empty-state check now requires all three of peers, orgs, and families to be empty before the no-tree-yet panel renders.

Final state: one commit (83c0f2e), five files touched (peopleTreeLayout.ts + test, PeopleTree.tsx, PeopleTabBody.tsx, HomeScreen.tsx — a one-line wallet.keyHistory pass-through). All four gates green throughout — typecheck silent, lint silent, 335 of 335 tests in 9.46s (gained 7 new tests this cut), build clean with HomeScreen bundle at 22.17KB gz still under the 22.5KB budget the prior session bumped to.
narrative.whats_pending:
Field-testing the tree-v2 family ring on the operator's actual phone is the honest next move — they should see their existing family or families they form land on the rose-tinted ring with the right name and the right signed-count, and the empty-state copy should not show when only families are present. Adding a family alone (no peers, no orgs) is a path the substrate now supports and that I have not visually verified.

WalletProvider.tsx remains at 797 lines, one under the 800 hard limit. The next touch to that file must include an extraction. The candidates the prior carpenter named are still the same — useInboxSubscription (the Mycelium subscription + handler wiring), useChatSubscription (the chat-thread substrate), or usePeerOps (the sendEnvelope + syncEnvelope + removePeerConnection + unholdEnvelope cluster). Worth pulling before the next transport-layer cut comes along and forces a less-considered extraction under time pressure.

The rotated-key bridge in family-unit signature detection is still one-sided. familySignatureProgress + memberHasSigned accept a keyAliases map, but every consumer (FamilyIdentitySections, FamilyRatifyModal, the new extractFamilies in PeopleTree) only populates it with the operator's own wallet.keyHistory. Other named members who rotate their keys after signing would still show as unsigned on the founder's wallet — the founder does not know remote peers' keyHistories. The proper fix would either embed a succession-proof leaf in the cosigned envelope at sign time (the cosigning member discloses their alias chain in the same envelope they sign) or have wallets publish a separate succession-link envelope that peers hold. Out of scope for this session, still flagged.

A polish thread on the tree-v2 family node: tapping a family node does not currently open anything. The natural extension is tap-for-detail — open FamilyIdentitySections or the new FamilyRatifyModal in view-only mode so the operator can see who is named, who has signed, who has not, and re-trigger the send-to-awaiting-members affordance. That belongs in the v3 maturation cut alongside the other named open tree threads (angular sector grouping by category, zoom + collapse, multi-hop expansion of friends-of-friends, org-chain walking via walkOrgChain, tap-a-peer-for-detail).

Add-birthday-now sibling cut for the operator's own missing-birthday pain point still waits. Same supplement-credential pattern the family-unit substrate established — a credential signed today carrying a backdated as_of leaf for the actual past date — closes it.

Four substrate-side back-burner candidates remain: receiveSelfMembership orgSelfDecl-lookup centralization, JoinOrgModal proof-candidate finder extraction, Phase D charter-amendment chain, and the appcommander metadata cleanup chip.
narrative.what_you_could_do_better:
Two honest observations. First, the family-unit edge color I picked aliases CATEGORY_COLOR.family — same pink as the family peer-category edge. The argument for sharing the color is visual cohesion (family-shaped relationships look family-shaped across both forms). The argument against is potential visual confusion: a peer with a family-relationship leaf draws a pink edge to the inner peer ring at the same color a family-unit envelope draws to the family ring. The structural distinction (radius + node shape) does the disambiguation work, but a reviewer looking at the screenshot for the first time might need a moment to parse which pink is which. An alternative I considered was a darker rose for family-units (rose-700 hex) to indicate 'this is a stronger multi-person unit' rather than 'this is a one-on-one family-typed peer.' I went with the alias because the family-mode arc's whole framing is that a family-unit and a family-peer-relationship are two views of the same fact at different levels of structure, and the shared color reinforces that. If field-testing surfaces confusion, the swap to a distinct darker rose is one constant.

Second, I did not add per-member-bubble rendering inside or alongside the family node. The chip-form question I asked named 'Branch family-unit nodes into their members under the operator's center node' as the cut, which implies the members would be rendered too. I shipped the family node alone — name + progress chip — and left the members as a count rather than individual bubbles. The reasoning: rendering per-member bubbles around each family node requires another layout decision (sub-ring of small bubbles around the family node? Connected by sub-edges to the family node? Or to the operator's center?), and the family-mode arc as it stands already shows each member on the inner peer ring via their handshake. Showing them twice (once on the peer ring, once around the family node) would double-render. Showing them once around the family node and removing them from the peer ring breaks the peer-ring's invariant that every handshake-known person appears there. The smallest useful version is the family node alone; the per-member rendering is a v3 maturation thread alongside the tap-for-detail flow that lets the operator open the family from the tree.

Nothing else surfaced beyond the declared scope this session.
narrative.bigger_picture:
The bigger-picture teaching this session is what 'extractor + renderer separation' buys for spatial visualizations. The PeopleTree v1 substrate the previous carpenter shipped established a clean boundary: peopleTreeLayout.ts owns the pure math (what to show, where, in what color), PeopleTree.tsx owns the rendering (SVG edges, positioned div nodes, IdentityChip reuse). Adding the family ring this session was almost mechanical because the boundary held — the layout module gained one new exported function (extractFamilies) and one new color constant, the renderer gained one new ring radius and one new node-render block, and the wiring layer (PeopleTabBody, HomeScreen) gained one new prop. No layout logic leaked into rendering; no rendering logic leaked into layout. The seven new tests landed on the pure-logic side where they belong (no jsdom React rendering, no I/O, no time-of-day dependence) and the visual side stays inspectable by eye in the running app. The pattern will repeat for the v3 maturation cuts: angular sector grouping by category is layout work, tap-for-detail is rendering-and-interaction work, multi-hop expansion is both (substrate for who's in scope, rendering for how to draw them). The boundary will hold for those too if we keep cutting on it.

The second teaching is what 'one substrate, three views' means at the family-mode layer. The same family-unit envelope now drives three operator-visible surfaces: FamilyIdentitySections on the Identity tab (full detail, per-member signed labels, founder-side send-to-members button), FamilyRatifyModal on the People tab when a member-side envelope arrives (review-and-ratify-with-one-tap), and the new family ring node in PeopleTree (aggregate-progress chip in a single rose tile). All three call into the same familyUnit.ts helpers — readFamilyUnit, familySignatureProgress, memberHasSigned with the keyAliases bridge. None of the three duplicates substrate logic. Each surface picks its level of detail (full / interactive / aggregate) and the substrate provides exactly that level. This is the Tapit Wallet doctrine of 'one envelope, one truth, many honest views' in action.

The broader thesis-level connection is the same Layer 4 framing every session keeps reinforcing. The operator who taps the People-tab Tree view and sees their family land as a rose tile labeled 'The Hearth · 2 of 3 signed' is reading the actual cryptographic state of their wallet — there is no caching layer, no derived metadata, no separate database of family relationships. The tile reads the holdings list every render and computes the answer fresh from the envelope signatures. If the third member ratifies tomorrow, the founder's wallet will absorb the cosignature and the tile will flip emerald the next time the operator opens the tab — automatically, with no further state plumbing, because the truth lives in the envelope itself and the surface is a window onto the envelope. That is what a sovereign-identity wallet earns when the cryptographic substrate is the single source of truth: the UI does not lie, because there is nothing for it to lie about that is not already crystallized in the signed bytes.

feedback_to_appcommander: The dispatch sandbox PFOR-016 protocol continued to hold cleanly this session. The brief named the branch claude/multisig-orgs-status-jiLwm and I stayed on it throughout. The close hook from the prior session resolved an interesting race I want to flag: when the close hook fires AFTER the carpenter's final reply but BEFORE the next session opens, the stop-hook-git-check.sh can flag unpushed commits one moment and be obsolete the next. The transient state is fine — the close hook resolves it within seconds — but a carpenter mid-reply might see the flag and assume action is needed. The honest answer is the close hook has it covered; the carpenter does not need to manually push for the comms checkpoint. One suggestion for the doctrine: name explicitly that stop-hook-git-check.sh races are expected and self-resolving, so future carpenters do not reflexively push the dispatch branch a second time.
